subject: Biology
title: Ribosomes: Protein Factories
description: A micro-lesson that makes Ribosomes: Protein Factories usable.

hook.text: Ribosomes read messenger RNA and stitch amino acids into proteins, one by one.

buildup.text: A single cell can contain millions of ribosomes, all building proteins at once.

discovery.text: They're made of RNA and protein, assembled in the nucleolus, then shipped out to work.

twist.text: Antibiotics like erythromycin jam bacterial ribosomes without harming yours.

climax.text: Every enzyme, hormone, and structural fiber in your body was built by a ribosome.

punchline.text: Tiny machines that build everything alive.

quiz.question: How do some antibiotics fight bacteria?

details.summary: Ribosomes are molecular machines that read mRNA instructions and assemble amino acids into proteins. They consist of two subunits made of ribosomal RNA and proteins and can be found free in the cytoplasm or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum.
details.whyItMatters: Ribosomes translate genetic code into functional proteins that build and operate every cell. Many antibiotics work by targeting bacterial ribosomes specifically, exploiting structural differences from human ribosomes to kill bacteria without harmi...
takeaways: Ribosomes read mRNA codons and assemble corresponding amino acid chains
Free ribosomes make cytoplasmic proteins; bound ribosomes make exported ones
Many antibiotics selectively target bacterial ribosomes to fight infections

faq.question: How do antibiotics target bacterial ribosomes without harming human cells?
faq.answer: Bacterial ribosomes are structurally different from eukaryotic ribosomes. Antibiotics like tetracycline and erythromycin bind bacterial ribosome structures that human ribosomes lack, selectively blocking bacterial protein synthesis while leaving human translation unaffected.

faq.question: How fast do ribosomes assemble proteins?
faq.answer: Bacterial ribosomes add about 20 amino acids per second, while eukaryotic ribosomes are slightly slower at about 6 per second. Multiple ribosomes can read the same mRNA simultaneously, called a polysome, dramatically increasing protein production speed.
